title: The Intersection of the Noble Eight-fold Path and the Precepts
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart's talk highlights the importance of integrating Buddhist teachings into daily life through two complementary frameworks: the Eightfold Path and the Zen Presets. These frameworks emphasize the interconnectedness of mindfulness, compassion, wisdom, and love, encouraging practitioners to cultivate wholesome intentions and act with kindness towards themselves and others. By embracing these principles, individuals can develop a more compassionate and awakened way of living, grounded in a deep understanding of the interconnectedness of all beings.

It is said that King Bimbisara was the one who suggested to the Buddha that his ordained disciples teach on full moon days so that lay people can learn from them.

Once monks recite the Patimokka, which was the Buddhist rule book of the time, and monks teach the Dhamma to lay people.
This was the start of the Buddhist full moon practices that continue to this day.
What fascinates me is that at the very beginning of the Buddha teaching in the world, there were no rules of conduct.
It was just a small group of close friends and Dharma practitioners practicing together.
They knew the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path, and that was enough.
So what are the Four Noble Truths?
The Truth of Dukkha, which is often translated as suffering.
The Truth of the Cause of Dukkha.
The Truth of the Cessation of Dukkha.
And the Truth of the Way leading to the Cessation of Dukkha, which is the Noble Eightfold Path.
We all experience Dukkha.
The Buddha himself said, "Monks, there are three kinds of suffering."
What three?
Suffering caused by pain.
Suffering caused by the formations or conditioned existence.
The suffering due to change.
It is for the full comprehension, clear understanding, ending and abandonment of these three forms of suffering that the Noble Eightfold Path is to be cultivated.
A little side note: please do not believe when Facebook says that the Buddha said life is suffering.
He didn't say that.
End of side note.
So what are the eight folds of the Eightfold Path?
Right View.
Our actions do have consequences; this is not the end, and our actions and beliefs have consequences even after our death.
Later, Right View came to explicitly include karma and rebirth.
Right Resolve or Right Intention.
The giving up of home and adopting the life of a religious mendicant in order to follow the path.
This concept aims at peaceful renunciation into an environment of non-sensuality, non-ill-will to loving kindness and away from cruelty to compassion.
In the beginning, in the Buddha's time, the serious practice was mostly for the monks and later for the monks and nuns.
The lay people, their job was to support the monks and nuns; that was their practice in that life.

No lying, no rude speech.
No telling one person what another says about him to cause discord or harm.
No idle chatter.
Right conduct or right action.
No killing, no injuring, no taking what is not giving, no sexual misconduct, no material desires.
I think you can see in the Eightfold Path how the presets are showing up.
Right Livelihood.
No trading in weapons, living beings, including slaves, meat, liquor or poisons.
Right Effort.
Preventing the arising of unwholesome states and generating wholesome states, including the seven factors of awakening.
This includes guarding the sense doors, restrained of the sense faculties.
Right Mindfulness.
The quality that guards or watches over the mind.
The stronger it becomes, the weaker unwholesome states of mind become, weakening the power to take over and dominate thought, word and deed.
To be conscious of what one is doing, the awareness of the impermanence of body, feeling and mind.
To experience the five aggregates, five hindrances.
Right Samadhi.
Right Meditation, which includes awakening, equanimity and mindfulness.

Then the Sangha of the Buddha became bigger.
More and more people found their way to him and wanted to practice with him.

So first a little bit about Bodhisattvas.
The idea of Bodhisattva is not unique to Mahayana Buddhism, but the meaning of Bodhisattva, as we know it in our tradition, is different from what was practiced in the early schools.
In the early schools, the belief was to be a Bodhisattva, to become a Bodhisattva; it was necessary that the future Buddhahood was predicted by a current living Buddha.
In Mahayana, in opposition to that, a Bodhisattva is any person from the moment they intend to become a Buddha, the arising of Bodhicitta.
And we do not have the requirement that a living Buddha must predict our Buddhahood.
Some Mahayana sutras, such as the Lotus Sutra, promote the Bodhisattva path as universal and open to everyone.
That is the beautiful aspect of the Lotus Sutra, the salvation aspect.
The Buddha promised everybody present while the Lotus Sutra was being taught, "You too will be a Buddha one day."
So we have 16 Bodhisattva precepts.
They are a set of vows of ethical conduct, taken many times in a Zen life.
They come originally from the Vinaya, those many, many rules, and they are vows of conduct taken on ordination.
When you take Jukai, you vow to follow the precepts.
When you ordain, you vow to follow the precepts, and at your funeral, someone vows that you will follow the precepts.
It's very sweet to have the precepts.

So the ten grave precepts, the one that says no killing, no stealing, etc., the ten grave precepts come pretty much straight forward from the Brahma Jala Sutra, as translated by Kumarachiva around 400 CE.
So the Bodhisattva precepts that we cherish emphasize conduct that benefits others, and it's taken by monastics and Zen practitioners, lay persons alike.

So, like I said a few minutes ago, the precepts form the basis of our ceremonies, and it's good to have those reminders to celebrate the full moon ceremony.
They're not just rules, they're lifetime koans.
And one thing that I especially love about our Zen precepts is I can only apply them to myself.
I cannot say, "Oh, so-and-so broke the precepts," because I don't know enough to speak that way.
So, the precepts support us through the living moment-to-moment awareness of our Zazen in our Zen practice.
They help direct us in our daily life of work, family, and relationships.
We remember them and we chant the precepts in a ceremony of reflection when the full moon rises, or once a month like we do here.
It's a beautiful ceremony that asks us to reflect on our conduct, to cherish repentance and renewal.
The April path, as taught by the Buddha, is a path that leads to the cessation of suffering.
It consists of the interconnected aspects.
Similarly, in Soto Zen Buddhism, the precepts serve as ethical guidelines.
They're not commandments to be blindly followed, but rather principles to be lived with and lived through, embodied in our daily lives.
Virtues such as non-harming, honesty, generosity, compassion, and mindfulness form the foundation of our ethical conduct.
They can guide us to a harmonious and compassionate relationship with all beings.
So how does this mesh together with our life?
Right view and right understanding encourage us to see and understand the nature of existence as impermanent, interdependent, devoid of a fixed self, non-duality, right intention.
And the precepts cultivate wholesome intentions and acting with a compassionate heart.
Both paths guide us to purify our intentions and to act with kindness, empathy, and goodwill towards ourselves and others.
The aspect of right speech and the precepts regarding speech highlight the power of our words.
They remind us to use speech that is truthful, kind, and beneficial.
By cultivating awareness and mindfulness, we become more attuned to the consequences of our speech, fostering a sense of responsibility and integrity.
Right livelihood and precepts remind us of the importance of engaging in work and actions that are aligned with our values and to not harm others.
Right effort teaches us the significance of diligent practice, which also accords with cherishing Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Both paths encourage us to find livelihoods and conduct supporting the well-being and happiness of all.
Right effort, again, asks us to develop a mind that is clear, focused, and free from afflictions.

Both precepts and the Eightfold Path emphasize the cultivation of present-moment awareness to develop a deep and sustained mindfulness, to be fully present as much as we can in every moment, to observe our thoughts, emotions, and actions without judgment or attachment.
Lastly, right concentration and right meditation guide us towards developing a focused and tranquil mind.
They teach us to let go of destruction, to cultivate deep concentration, and to experience the transformative power of silence and stillness.
As we reflect on this and study this, we should recognize that these paths complement each other, and they are leading us to the same destination.
By integrating these teachings, we harmonize wisdom, ethics, and mindfulness, nurturing a holistic approach.

So while the Eightfold Path provides a more comprehensive framework for the development of our morality, wisdom, and meditation, the precepts speak much more to the specifics, to the day-to-day steps of our life.
So maybe, since I talked a lot, it would help if I just bring up real quickly the comparison.
Ethical conduct provides guidelines for refraining from harmful actions such as killing, stealing, lying—there's the precepts.
Mindfulness, cultivation of mindfulness, and present moment awareness.
The precepts aim more at the embodiment of mindfulness in everyday life, while the Eightfold Path definitely includes mindfulness as one of the aspects.
Comprehensive versus concise, the Eightfold Path is like the large umbrella that covers the comprehensive framework of our spiritual development, ethical conduct, wisdom, and meditation.
And in contrast, the Zen precepts offer more concise guidelines focused on ethical conduct.

And then the formality, that's more a function of the precepts, because we do specifically engage with them in our full moon ceremony and our great ceremonies, chokai and oilination, and those great markers in our lives.
I would like to close with another Mary Oliver poem.
It's called Invitation.
*Oh, do you have time to linger for just a little while out of your busy and very important day?
For the goldfinches have gathered in a field of thistles.
For a musical battle to see who can sing the highest note or the lowest, or the most expressive of mirth or the most tender?
Their strong blunt beaks drink the air as they strive melodiously, not for your sake and not for mine, and not for the sake of winning, but for sheer delight and gratitude.
Believe us, they say, it is a serious thing just to be alive on this fresh morning in the broken world.
I beg of you, do not walk by without passing to attend to this rather ridiculous performance.*
It could mean something.
It could mean everything.
It could be what Wilke meant when he wrote, "You must change your life."
Thank you very much.
May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
